metadata.title: Fortinet's AI Surge Is Impressive. Is Microsoft Stock The Smarter Way In?

content.text:
Both companies are riding the AI infrastructure boom, but Microsoft offers that exposure with faster growth and a cheaper valuation, forcing a hard look at what Fortinet's premium price is buying you from here.
If you own a major systems software stock, you likely own it for one reason right now: the historic build-out of artificial intelligence. This wave of investment demands a new layer of security and computing infrastructure, a tide lifting many boats. Fortinet (FTNT) and Microsoft (MSFT) are two of the most direct ways to own this theme. A reader holding one is making an implicit choice over the other.
That choice has become stark. Over the last 3 months, Fortinet has rocketed up 112%, while Microsoft has returned +0.4%. The obvious read is that the focused cybersecurity player has the hot hand. But for an investor deciding what to own from here, the forward-looking picture is more complicated, and the decision turns on which company's story better supports its price tag.
The Demand: Both Are Drinking From The AI Firehose
Both companies are squarely in the path of AI-driven spending. Fortinet's management is clear: "AI is a tailwind to drive the growth." They are seeing this in demand for securing new AI data centers and in protecting critical infrastructure, where operational technology (OT) billings grew over 70%. The company is winning large deals, with the number of contracts over $1 million growing and total deal value growing over 60% in its last quarter.
Microsoft's exposure is even more direct. It both secures the AI boom and builds its very foundation. The company reported its "AI business surpassed $37 billion ARR, up 123%." Its Microsoft Cloud division, the engine of its growth, exceeded $54 billion in quarterly revenue. For both companies, the core demand story is powerful and intact. The question is how efficiently each is converting that demand into a durable investment case.
The Forward Signal: A Raised Guide vs. A Massive Investment
The cleanest signal of management's confidence is its own guidance. Here, Fortinet makes a strong statement. In its latest report, the company raised its full-year 2026 guidance for revenue and service revenue. A company actively lifting its own forecast is a clear vote of confidence in its near-term order book.
Microsoft's forward signal is one of staggering scale. It expects "another year of double-digit revenue and operating income growth in FY '27." But underpinning that growth is a colossal spending plan. Management expects to invest roughly $190 billion in capital expenditures in calendar year 2026. This is the core risk an investor accepts: you are underwriting a capital investment cycle of historic proportions, betting it will translate into the profitable growth Microsoft projects.
The Twist: The High-Flyer Is The Pricier, Slower Grower
Here is where the story turns. Despite Fortinet's explosive stock performance, the trailing numbers challenge the idea that it is the superior growth story. Microsoft is actually growing faster, with 17.9% revenue growth over the last twelve months versus 15.7% for Fortinet. Microsoft is also significantly more profitable, with a 47% operating margin compared to Fortinet's 31%.
Yet Fortinet is the far more expensive stock. It trades at a price-to-operating-income multiple of 50.5, while Microsoft trades at a more modest 18.2. This contrast between a focused security player and a tech giant raises a key question, one we have explored in more detail before. For an investor today, you are paying a much higher premium for Fortinet's growth, which is currently slower and less profitable than Microsoft's. Fortinet's raised guidance is what bulls are counting on to close that gap.
The Verdict: Which Way Does The Evidence Lean?
On the evidence, Microsoft currently presents a cleaner way to own the AI infrastructure theme. It offers faster growth, superior margins, and a more compelling valuation. Its moat, built on the deep integration of its Azure cloud platform with enterprise workflows through Microsoft Copilot, creates immense switching costs. For investors who want exposure to the broader software theme without picking a single name, a sector ETF that owns both could be an alternative.
Investing in Microsoft from here means betting that its $190 billion capital plan will pay off. As one analyst on its earnings call noted, there is "a bit of a disconnect that makes investors a bit nervous between how fast they're seeing CapEx growing and how fast they're seeing revenue growing." That is the central risk.
Fortinet's bull case rests on its focused execution, market share gains in cybersecurity, and that freshly raised guidance. Its moat is its single, integrated operating system, FortiOS 8.0, and its custom FortiASIC chips that it argues provide a performance edge. The risk is that its high valuation leaves no room for error. An analyst on the call raised the specter of a post-COVID style "air pocket" if the current demand is a temporary pull-forward. At 50.5 times operating income, any slowdown could be painful.
Ultimately, the choice turns on what you are more comfortable underwriting: Microsoft's massive, but potentially high-return, capital spending, or Fortinet's premium valuation in the hope its focused momentum can be sustained. The smarter move isn't to chase the hot stock, but to ask which of these forward-looking bargains you truly believe in.

You can line Fortinet and Microsoft up directly on the Fortinet peer comparison, weigh them on valuation, growth, margins, and returns, and swap in any other Systems Software names you hold.
What Would You Do With A Gain Like FTNT's 225%?
A comparison sharpens the pick, but owning too much of either name is the same concentrated bet. FTNT is up 225% over the past five years, and gains like that are exactly how one holding quietly becomes too large a share of a portfolio.
